chunks.label: Can, be done, make do
chunks.rationale: The four voice forms: can (potential), be done (passive), make or let (causative), be made to (causative-passive). They are all built the same way, a vowel change plus -reru or -seru, so they are easiest to tell apart side by side.
chunks.interference: Ichidan potential and passive are identical (taberareru, mirareru), and kuru gives korareru for both. -aseru (make do) and -areru (be done) differ by one sound, and -asareru stacks both.

chunks.label: Commands
chunks.rationale: Ways to tell someone to do or not do something, from rough (ike, iku na) to parental (-nasai) to blunt but personal (-te kure). You mostly hear these; for your own requests, -te and -te kudasai do the job.
chunks.interference: The command ike sounds like the potential ikeru; ike (go!) and iku na (don't go!) are opposites built on the same verb. -nasai sounds soft but talks down.

chunks.label: Helper verbs after -te
chunks.rationale: Each is the te-form plus a small verb or particle: -te shimau, -te oku, -te miru, -te mo. Two of them shrink in speech (-chau, -toku), so the full and short forms are learned together.
chunks.interference: -toku (do ahead) vs -teku (-te iku); -chau (end up) vs -cha (-te wa, must not); -te mo (even if) vs -te miru (try).

chunks.label: Doing two things
chunks.rationale: Three ways to fit two actions in one sentence: as examples (-tari), at the same time (-nagara), or one without the other (-zu ni).
chunks.interference: Each takes a different stem: -tari the past (tabetari), -nagara the -masu stem (tabenagara), -zu ni the negative stem (tabezu ni). Mixing the stems is the usual slip.

chunks.label: Looks, too much, easy
chunks.rationale: All three hang off the -masu stem: tabesou, tabesugiru, tabeyasui. One stem, three common add-ons.
chunks.interference: Stem + sou (looks like) vs dictionary form + sou da (I hear); -yasui (easy to) vs yasui (cheap).

chunks.label: Spoken shortcuts
chunks.rationale: Fast casual speech squeezes sounds: wakannai, -teru, -nakya, -chau. These are what make real conversation hard to follow, so each is learned as a map back to its full form.
chunks.interference: -cha (-te wa) vs -chau (-te shimau); -nakya (must) vs -nai (not); the -n of wakannai vs the n of n da.

chunks.label: Adjectives and the copula
chunks.rationale: The core shapes of adjectives and nouns: is, was, isn't, wasn't, probably. i-adjectives change their own ending; na-adjectives and nouns lean on da, desu and deshou.
chunks.interference: Polite past is -katta desu, not -i deshita; ii becomes yo- in every changed form (yokatta, yokunai); da never follows an i-adjective.

chunks.label: Adjectives that link and change
chunks.rationale: What adjectives do inside a longer sentence: link (-kute / de), change (-ku naru), sit before a noun (na / no), set a condition (-kattara), and say how things look (-sou).
chunks.interference: -ku naru (becomes) vs -ku suru (makes it); stem + sou (looks) vs plain + sou da (I hear); ii → yokute, yoku, yosasou.
